# Viva sheet: concept questions. Learn the ideas, then answer in YOUR words. Numbers auto-filled from real runs.

**1. How is attacking ReID different from attacking a classifier?**
A classifier outputs a label; ReID outputs an embedding and is scored on the ranking of a gallery. So the useful objective is in embedding space (distance/cosine to the clean or a target embedding), not cross-entropy on a label. Test identities are never seen in training, so the classifier head is not even used at test time. Our measurement: PGD in embedding space gives Rank-1 0.0, classifier-style Logit-PGD gives 0.3.

**2. What are evasion and impersonation?** Evasion: make the query stop matching its true identity (minimise cosine to its own clean embedding). Impersonation: make it match a chosen identity (maximise cosine to that identity's centroid).

**3. Why is normalisation inside the model?** So the epsilon budget (8/255) is measured on raw pixels in [0,1]; otherwise the effective perturbation would depend on mean/std scaling.

**4. FGSM vs PGD vs MI-FGSM?** FGSM: one step of size eps along the gradient sign. PGD: several smaller steps (here alpha = 2.5*eps/steps), random start, project into the eps-ball after each step. MI-FGSM: accumulates an L1-normalised gradient with momentum, stabilising direction; designed to improve transfer.

**5. Why do we project and clip?** To satisfy ||delta||_inf <= eps and keep pixels valid in [0,1]; we assert this in code for every batch.

**6. White-box vs black-box transfer?** White-box = gradients of the victim itself (diagonal of the matrix). Transfer = craft on a surrogate, test on another model (off-diagonal). Mean Rank-1 after PGD: white-box 0.0, transfer 61.0.

**7. Why might attacks transfer?** Models trained on the same data can learn similar decision-relevant features, so perturbations that hurt one may hurt another. Why transfer differs between CNN->CNN and CNN->ViT is a hypothesis unless tested; say what the heat-map shows and label explanations as hypotheses.

**8. What is EOT?** Expectation over Transformation: optimise the patch on average over random scale/rotation/shift/lighting/noise so it keeps working when conditions change, instead of overfitting one exact placement.

**9. What is "universal" about the patch?** One patch for all images (no per-image optimisation). Loss needs no labels: minimise similarity between patched and clean embeddings of the same image.

**10. Why the random-patch control?** To show the drop comes from the learned pattern, not just from covering part of the torso: random 73.2 vs trained 2.7 Rank-1 on ResNet-50.

**11. Why total-variation loss?** Smooth patches are more printable/camera-robust than high-frequency noise.

**12. What is the Market-1501 protocol and the junk rule?** Queries vs gallery from different cameras; gallery images with the same identity AND same camera as the query are ignored; report CMC (Rank-k) and mAP. Rank-1 = is the top result correct; mAP rewards ranking all true matches high.

**13. Why batch-hard triplet loss + PK sampler?** Triplet loss needs positives and negatives in every batch: P identities x K images guarantees both; picking the hardest positive/negative per anchor gives a strong learning signal. BNNeck separates the triplet feature from the ID-loss feature.

**14. What does adversarial training do and cost?** Trains on PGD examples (here a mix of clean and adversarial loss). Clean Rank-1 87.0 -> 74.5; under PGD 0.0 -> 29.2. Robustness usually costs clean accuracy; a defence evaluated only against the attack it was trained on can be over-optimistic.

**15. What are the limitations of your study?** One seed, one dataset, "epoch" = pass over identities not images, digital patch only (no printing/camera), white-box PGD evaluated with 10 steps, no adaptive attack against the defence.

**16. How do we know the numbers are real?** Every number is generated by scripts from JSON files; `results/MANIFEST.json` stores commit and checkpoint hashes; `scripts/verify_results.py` checks consistency.
